title: Every rerun starts cold
impact: Moonshot: accepted, and the finding is bigger than the code. A stream rerun runs on a reader connection only because a commit preceded it, and in WAL mode a connection that watches another connection commit begins its next statement by discarding its whole page cache and, with `mmap_size` set, unmapping the database file (`pager_reset`). Measured with no isolates: one hash pass on a reader after a commit costs 3.2x its warm cost on a 50-row index page (31.6 vs 9.7 us), 2.6-4.2x on a point read, and the same statement on the writer connection after its own commit costs 1.1x, because the writer wrote the header it compares against. Two hundred and eighty-eight experiments priced the hop, the hash and the messaging around a rerun; none had run it after a commit. Turning `mmap` off on readers (candidate A) halves the tax on one-page shapes and raises it a third on fifty-page ones -- point `select()` after a commit -26%, a 50-row page +32% -- so the pragma stays. Running the rerun on the writer connection when it is idle (candidate B) ships: a `RerunRequest` on the writer, one <= 256-row entry per flush round, gated on a caller-side count of writes in progress and decided in a microtask after the caller's continuation. Write-to-emission latency on a 50-row stream -34/-34/-33/-32% (74 -> 49 us), a one-row stream -20%, a three-statement transaction -26%, reproduced in four order-flipped passes, with sequential and concurrent write bursts, 50-stream fan-out and `write-only` flat. Two rejected shapes of the same idea are recorded because they measure the hazard: a microtask that reads only the writer's queues misreads every sequential write as idle and makes a 3.3 ms burst 8.7 ms; a `Timer.run` deferral reads them right and costs 2.5 us per timer.
